idiom_name: struct with let stored properties and value semantics
implementation_notes: Swift builds immutability into its type system for value types: a struct whose properties are declared let cannot be modified after initialisation, and assigning the struct to a let binding freezes all its properties together, including nested value types. Every assignment or argument pass behaves as a copy, with copy-on-write inside the standard collections keeping that cheap, and mutating methods must be marked mutating so they cannot be called on a let value. The class-with-no-setters form remains justified when reference identity is required (delegates, identity-based graphs) or for Objective-C interop.
pitfalls: let fixes only that instance: the same struct held in a var can be passed to a mutating method, so APIs should offer non-mutating counterparts (sorted() beside sort()) and values should be held as let.
A struct holding a class reference is only shallowly immutable: the referenced object can still mutate, so stored properties should themselves be value types or immutable references.

Copy-on-write is an implementation detail of Array, Dictionary and String rather than a language rule; a custom type holding a buffer reference must implement uniqueness checks (isKnownUniquelyReferenced) itself.
